46: You need a running total that starts at the right value, and then you visit every element once.
A for...of loop with a "total" variable works, and so does reduce. Pay attention to the starting value.
Start with total = 0, add each element to it, then return total. An empty array just gives the starting value back.
47: Picture reading the array from the last element back to the first one.
You can loop backwards, or copy the array first and then use the built-in .reverse() on the copy (.reverse() changes the array it is called on!).
Make a copy with [...arr] (or arr.slice()), then reverse the copy and return it. Or build a result array by looping i from arr.length - 1 down to 0.
48: Remember that numbers are not strings: 9 is smaller than 10, even though "9" comes after "10" alphabetically.
Array.prototype.sort accepts a compare function (a, b) => ... that tells it how two items should be ordered.
The compare function should return a negative number if a goes first, positive if b goes first. For ascending numbers, return a - b.
49: You are keeping some elements and dropping others. What question decides if an element stays?
filter() builds a new array from the elements that pass a test, so the original is left alone.
Keep an element when it is greater than or equal to 0: arr.filter(...) with that check.
50: Think about how you would find the tallest person in a line: remember the tallest one you have seen so far.
Keep a variable "max" and compare every element with it. Be careful what you start it with: 0 is not safe when every number is negative.
Start with max = arr[0]. Loop through the array and whenever an element is bigger than max, replace max. Return max at the end. (Math.max(...arr) also works.)
51: For each element, ask: "have I already kept this value?"
A Set only stores each value once, so it can do the "already seen" bookkeeping for you (and it remembers insertion order).
Turn the array into a Set and back into an array: [...new Set(arr)]. Or loop and push an element only if the result does not contain it yet.
52: Imagine two sorted queues: at each step, the next element of the merged result is one of the two front elements.
Keep one index per array (i and j). Compare a[i] with b[j], take the smaller one, and move that array's index forward.
Loop while both indexes are inside their arrays, pushing the smaller element each time. When one array runs out, push everything that is left in the other one.
53: This is two small jobs in one: join the arrays, then remove the duplicates.
A Set keeps each value only once. Spreading both arrays into one Set does both jobs at once.
Put all the elements of a and then b into a single array, build a Set from it, and spread the Set back into an array.
54: You want one output element for every input element, so the new array has the same length.
map() transforms every element with a function and returns a new array.
arr.map(x => ...) where the function returns x multiplied by itself.
55: Look at the elements one by one, from the start, and stop as soon as you find the one you want.
A classic for loop gives you the index i directly. Compare arr[i] with v using ===.
Loop i from 0 to arr.length - 1; as soon as arr[i] === v, return i. If the loop ends without finding anything, return -1.
56: Duplicates of the biggest number must not be mistaken for the second biggest. Think about how to get rid of them first.
Make the values unique (a Set helps), then either sort them from largest to smallest or track the top two in a loop.
Unique values sorted descending: the answer is the element at index 1. If that element does not exist, you get undefined for free.
57: If all elements are equal, then every one of them equals the first element. What if one of them does not?
every() returns true only when its test passes for all elements (and it returns true for an empty array).
arr.every(x => x === arr[0]). Or loop and return false at the first element that differs from arr[0]; return true after the loop.
58: You can compute both numbers in a single pass over the array, with two running variables.
A sum starts at 0 (adding nothing) and a product starts at 1 (multiplying by nothing). Those starting values also give you the answer for an empty array.
Set sum = 0 and product = 1, loop over the array doing sum += x and product *= x, then return { sum, product }.
59: To know which value is the most frequent you first need to know how many times each value appears.
Count with an object or a Map: the value is the key, the number of times you have seen it is the stored number.
Loop once to fill the counts. Then loop over the counts (or keep track while counting) and remember the value with the highest count.
60: A value is a duplicate if you meet it again after having seen it before. How can you remember what you have seen?
Use a Set (or a counts object) of the values seen so far. Careful: a value that appears three times must still be reported only once.
Count every value first. Then go through the unique values in first-seen order and keep the ones whose count is greater than 1.
61: An element is either a plain value or another array. An inner array is the same problem again, just smaller.
Recursion fits well: flatten each inner array with the same function. Array.isArray(item) tells you which case you are in. (There is also a built-in flat(), try writing it yourself first.)
Loop over arr with an empty result. If the item is an array, add everything returned by flatten(item); otherwise push the item.
62: Go through a and decide, element by element, whether it stays. The question is "is it in b?".
filter() keeps the elements that pass a test. The test can use b.includes(x) (or a Set built from b, which is faster for long arrays).
a.filter(x => !b.includes(x)). Remember the "!": you keep the elements that are NOT in b.
63: JavaScript can turn any value into true or false. Falsy values are the ones that become false.
filter() keeps an element when your test returns a truthy value. What if the element itself is the test result?
arr.filter(x => x), or arr.filter(Boolean): each element is kept exactly when it is truthy.
64: For each number, there is exactly one other number that would complete the sum. What is it?
The brute force way checks every pair with two nested loops. A faster way remembers earlier numbers (and their indexes) in a Map.
Loop through the array. For nums[i], compute need = target - nums[i]. If need was already seen earlier, return [thatIndex, i]; otherwise store nums[i] with its index.
65: Both functions return a piece of the array. Which built-in method cuts a piece out without changing the original?
slice(start, end) copies a section. Negative start values count from the end. Watch out for n = 0 in last(): slice(-0) is the same as slice(0).
first: arr.slice(0, n). last: arr.slice(-n), but return [] when n is 0 (or use arr.slice(Math.max(arr.length - n, 0))).
66: You need an array with exactly n slots, and every slot gets the same value.
You can start with an empty array and push in a loop, or create an array of length n and use the built-in fill().
new Array(n).fill(value) (or Array(n).fill(value)), or: loop i from 0 to n - 1 and push value each time.
67: Picture a deck of cards: you repeatedly pick a random card from the cards that are not yet "placed" and put it in the next position.
Fisher-Yates: walk the array from the end to the start; at each index i, pick a random index j between 0 and i and swap the two elements. Do it on a copy.
result = [...arr]; for i from result.length - 1 down to 1: j = Math.floor(Math.random() * (i + 1)); swap result[i] and result[j]. Return result.
68: Look at two neighbours at a time: if the left one is bigger than the right one, they are in the wrong order.
One pass of swapping neighbours pushes the biggest remaining number to the end ("bubbles up"). Repeat passes until nothing is left to swap.

Use two nested loops: the outer one shrinks the unsorted part by one each pass, the inner one compares arr[i] with arr[i + 1] and swaps them if arr[i] is bigger (use a temporary variable or destructuring to swap).
69: You take the array piece by piece: elements 0 to size-1, then size to 2*size-1, and so on.
A loop that jumps forward by size each time (i += size), together with slice(i, i + size), cuts out each chunk. slice is forgiving when you ask for more than is left.
result = []; for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i += size) push arr.slice(i, i + size) into result. Return result.
70: You are keeping every element except the ones that match. All matches go, not only the first one.
filter() builds a new array from the elements that pass a test, and leaves the original untouched.
arr.filter(x => x !== value): keep each element that is not equal to the value.
